SYSTEMS PROGRAMMING AND MACHINE ORGANIZATION
Chapter 23 — Paging
VERBATIM GRADUATE LECTURE TRANSCRIPT
Charles Dorner

SLIDE 1: Chapter 23 — Paging

LECTURE NARRATION
Paging divides virtual address spaces and physical storage into fixed-size units. This simplifies placement: a virtual page can be backed by any suitable physical frame of the corresponding size. It also makes translation arithmetic systematic. The system trades fine-grained flexibility against page-table overhead, internal waste, and translation-cache coverage. [ R10 ]

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, paging divides virtual address spaces and physical storage into fixed-size units.

SLIDE 4: 23.1 Pages

LECTURE NARRATION
A page is a fixed-size unit in the virtual address space. A mapping associates a virtual page with backing storage and permissions. Pages should not be confused with C objects: a page can contain many objects, part of one object, or bytes that no live language object currently occupies. A large allocation can span many pages. Crossing its internal page boundaries is valid when the allocation and mappings permit it. Conversely, staying within one page does not prove an array index is valid. Object-level bounds and page-level mapping boundaries solve different problems.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
The program uses a map of memory addresses. The operating system translates that map to where the data is actually stored.

========================================================================================

SLIDE 6: 23.2 Frames

LECTURE NARRATION
A frame is a page-sized unit of physical storage. The kernel tracks which frames are free, in use, shared, or involved in other memory-management activity. A virtual page number and a physical frame number need not be equal. The distinction makes noncontiguous physical placement possible. Three adjacent virtual pages can be backed by frames 5, 200, and 9 while still appearing contiguous to the application. Device operations requiring particular physical arrangements need additional platform mechanisms; virtual contiguity alone is not a guarantee of physical contiguity.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, a frame is a page-sized unit of physical storage.

SLIDE 8: 23.3 Page size

LECTURE NARRATION
For the following calculations, the page size is 4 KiB, or 4096 bytes. This is a teaching assumption, not a claim that every mapping on every system uses that size. Systems can support multiple page sizes, and applications should query the relevant platform interface where a runtime page size matters. Larger pages increase the amount of memory covered by one translation entry and reduce some table overhead. They can also waste more space for small or sparsely touched regions and complicate allocation or migration. The best size depends on workload and system policy, not merely on choosing the largest supported number.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
The program uses a map of memory addresses. The operating system translates that map to where the data is actually stored.

SLIDE 10: 23.4 Page offset

LECTURE NARRATION
For a page size of 2^p bytes, the low p address bits form the page offset. With 4096-byte pages, p = 12 . The offset is address mod 4096 , or equivalently address & 0xFFF for the nonnegative integer model. Translation preserves these low bits when mapping a page to an equal-sized frame. Only the page-number portion changes. This separation makes the final physical-address calculation straightforward and explains why correctly aligned page bases have zeroes in the offset positions.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
The program uses a map of memory addresses. The operating system translates that map to where the data is actually stored.

SLIDE 12: 23.5 Virtual page number

LECTURE NARRATION
The virtual page number is the address divided by page size, rounded down. In the bit model, it is address >> p . It identifies which page-table mapping applies, potentially through several levels of indexing. The number of bits available for the virtual page number depends on the virtual-address model. In a 32-bit model with 4-KiB pages, there are 20 virtual-page-number bits and 12 offset bits. Do not transfer those counts unchanged to a different address width or page size.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
The program uses a map of memory addresses. The operating system translates that map to where the data is actually stored.

SLIDE 14: 23.6 Physical page number

LECTURE NARRATION
The physical page number, also called a frame number in this discussion, identifies the selected frame. If the frame number is f , its base address is f * page_size . Add the original offset to obtain the final physical address. A page-table entry contains more than a frame number, so real software cannot treat every bit of an entry as an address. Flag bits and architecture-specific encodings must be interpreted correctly. The arithmetic below deliberately uses a dictionary of already-decoded frame numbers to isolate the translation concept.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
The program uses a map of memory addresses. The operating system translates that map to where the data is actually stored.

SLIDE 16: Worked example — A checked translation model

LECTURE NARRATION
For virtual address 0x12345 , the virtual page number is 0x12 and the offset is 0x345 . If page 0x12 maps to frame 0x2A , the physical address is 0x2A345 . Companion listing: ch23/paging.py The model intentionally excludes permissions, multilevel tables, TLBs, and demand paging. A missing dictionary entry raises an exception in the model; it does not simulate the kernel’s full page-fault policy. Keeping that boundary explicit prevents a useful arithmetic exercise from being mistaken for a complete MMU implementation.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, for virtual address 0x12345 , the virtual page number is 0x12 and the offset is 0x345 .

SLIDE 18: Worked example — Splitting a virtual address

LECTURE NARRATION
With 4 KiB pages, the page offset is 12 bits because 4096 = 2^12 . For virtual address 0x12345 , the offset is 0x345 and the virtual page number is 0x12 . Translation replaces the virtual page number with a physical frame number while preserving the offset.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
Think of an address written on a note: the note can tell you where to look, but it does not prove the thing is still there or that you are allowed to use it.

SLIDE 20: Worked example — Counting pages

LECTURE NARRATION
A 10,000-byte region starting on a page boundary spans ceil(10000/4096)=3 pages. If the region begins 3,000 bytes into a page, it consumes the remaining 1,096 bytes of that page plus enough later pages for the rest, so alignment of the start address can increase the number of pages touched.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION

SLIDE 22: Guided lab and review

LECTURE NARRATION
Lab 23. Change the model to 8-KiB pages in a 32-bit virtual and physical space. Recalculate the number of offset bits and the frame-number bound. Translate 0x12345 when its virtual page maps to frame 0x2A . Review 1. Can adjacent virtual pages use nonadjacent frames? Review 2. How much unused space can the last page of a nonempty byte region contain?

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SLIDE 24: Chapter Synthesis

LECTURE NARRATION
The chapter's central subject is paging. Correct reasoning requires explicit assumptions, bounds, ownership, and interface contracts. Observed behavior is evidence about a run; it is not automatically a language or system guarantee. Use the worked examples and lab to test whether the model transfers to new cases.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true.
